newsitem.title: INDIA: India, UK in diplomatic spat over cocktail invite.
newsitem.headline: India, UK in diplomatic spat over cocktail invite.

text.p: India on Wednesday chided Britain over a social invitation that New Delhi said showed diplomatic insensitivity, although the British ambassador said it was a storm in a teacup.
The invitation to a cocktail party at the British High Commission (embassy) on April 12 was to meet a diplomat whose title was given as First Secretary (Foreign Policy and Kashmir).

Foreign Ministry officials and the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) reacted angrily to the separate mention of the Kashmir region, part of which is in India's Jammu and Kashmir state. Pakistan rules over the other one third.
The BJP said in a statement the designation "implies that the British High Commission has decided to deal with Kashmir as a separate entity and not as a part of (the) Indian union".

"It is a gross violation of India's territorial integrity and an unacceptable diplomatic offensive by a foreign mission based in this country. It is tantamount to insulting the host nation and interfering in India's internal affairs," the rightwing Hindu party said.
New Delhi says Kashmir, including the section controlled by Pakistan, is an integral part of the Indian nation.
A Foreign Ministry official said the inclusion of Kashmir in the diplomat's title "smacks of a certain ignorance of the situation in India and insensitivity of the overall situation in South Asia.
"I suspect it may be an error. I hope it is an error," he told reporters.
Kashmir was the cause of two of the three wars that India and Pakistan have fought since 1947, and each country still stakes a claim to the entire region.
British High Commissioner David Gore-Booth said in a statement that there had been no change in British policy towards Kashmir and no new post had been created.

He said the diplomat's title was First Secretary (Chancery), and she specialises in India's foreign policy and coordinates the high commission's efforts to establish the fate of two British nationals taken hostage in Kashmir in July 1995.

Britons Keith Mangan and Paul Wells were among six Western tourists captured by separatist guerrillas in the Himalayan region. One escaped, another was beheaded and Mangan and Wells, along with an American and a German, remain unaccounted for.
Gore-Booth said the invitations summarised the diplomat's duties so guests would know something about her portfolio before meeting her. "This appears to be a storm in a teacup," he said.
